content:
This week I focused on defining the idea behind MyOllama and establishing what I wanted the application to achieve.
The main goal is to create a backend application that allows users to generate short quiz videos by selecting a category. The application should automatically generate a question, create answer options, produce speech and combine the necessary media into a finished video.
I started by breaking the project into smaller components: user accounts, authentication, quiz generation, audio generation, media resources and video rendering.
This helped me understand how the different services would need to communicate. I also began thinking about the order of the workflow, from receiving a user’s request to returning the completed MP4 file.
Next week I will focus on the technical architecture and the technologies needed to make the application work.
title: Project Kickoff and Defining the Idea

title: About

content:
This week I focused on the technical architecture of MyOllama. I worked on deciding how the backend should be structured and which technologies would be suitable for the project.
I chose Java with Javalin for the backend because it provides a lightweight way to create HTTP endpoints without introducing an unnecessarily large framework.
I also planned a layered architecture. Routes define the available endpoints, controllers handle incoming requests, services communicate with external systems and DAO classes are responsible for database operations.
The project uses Maven for dependency management, PostgreSQL and Hibernate for persistence, and Java’s HttpClient for communication with external APIs.
I also identified the main external services: Ollama for generating quiz content, Kokoro for text-to-speech and FFmpeg for video rendering.
This gave me a much clearer overview of how the application should work. Next week I will focus on the project structure and data models.
title: Choosing the Architecture and Technologies

content:
This week I worked on organising the codebase and planning the data models used throughout MyOllama.
I focused on separating the different responsibilities into packages for routes, controllers, services, data access, entities and DTOs. This makes the code easier to maintain and helps prevent individual classes from becoming responsible for too many things.
I also worked through the main entities. The Client represents a registered user, while the video workflow uses objects such as Video, VideoFile, VideoInstruction and VideoRequest.
These objects are important because generating a video requires several different resources. The application needs to handle images, audio files, text overlays and instructions before sending everything to the rendering service.
I also considered how information should move between the different layers of the application.
Next week I will focus on connecting the database and implementing the first parts of the user registration system.
title: Project Structure and Data Modelling

content:
This week I focused on the database and user registration functionality.
I worked with PostgreSQL and Hibernate to establish the persistence layer and organise how client information is stored. The Client entity is central to this part of the application because users need an account before accessing protected functionality.
I also worked on registration validation. The application needs to reject invalid usernames, passwords that are too short and usernames that already exist in the database.
An important part of this work was password security. Instead of storing passwords as plain text, I used BCrypt to hash them before saving them.
I also looked at the difference between the website registration flow and the JSON API registration flow. They have different request formats, so it is important that both are handled consistently.
The registration foundation is now clearer. Next week I will focus on login, authentication tokens and access control.
title: Database Setup and User Registration

content:
This week I focused on authentication and security in MyOllama.
I worked on the login functionality and the use of JSON Web Tokens. After a successful login, the application can issue a JWT that the client can use when accessing protected endpoints.
The API uses Bearer tokens in the Authorization header, while the website flow can also use an HTTP-only authentication cookie.
I also worked with role-based access control. The project defines three roles: ANYONE, STANDARD and PREMIUM. These roles make it possible to restrict certain endpoints depending on the user’s permissions.
For example, video generation requires an authenticated standard-level user, while premium users can access standard-level functionality as well.
One important thing I learned is that authentication and authorisation are two separate concerns. First the application needs to establish who the user is, and then it needs to check whether that user is allowed to perform the requested action.
Next week I will focus on connecting Ollama and generating quiz questions.
title: Authentication, JWT and User Roles

content:
This week I focused on the quiz-generation functionality.
MyOllama uses the Ollama API together with the Qwen 2.5 3B model to generate multiple-choice questions based on a category provided by the user.
I worked on the prompt structure to make the generated responses more predictable. The model needs to return one question, four possible answers labelled A to D and one correct answer.
The OllamaService handles communication with the external API. It uses Java’s HttpClient to send the request and Jackson to process the JSON response into a structured DTO.
This is important because the rest of the application needs to work with the generated question and answers in a consistent format.
I also realised that prompt design has a direct effect on the reliability of the application. If the response format changes unexpectedly, the later stages of the video workflow can become more difficult.
Next week I will focus on converting the generated text into audio and collecting the media resources needed for the video.
title: Connecting Ollama and Generating Quiz Questions

content:
This week I worked on the audio generation and media resource parts of MyOllama.
After Ollama generates a quiz question and its answers, the application needs spoken versions of the relevant text. I worked with the Kokoro text-to-speech service, which receives text through a JSON request and returns audio data in WAV format.
I also looked at how the application retrieves additional resources. These include the background image, countdown sound and background music.
The ResourceService is responsible for communicating with the resource server. This keeps the resource-related HTTP requests separate from the main controller logic.
At this stage, the workflow is becoming more complete. The application can generate quiz content, prepare speech and collect the media files that will eventually be combined into a video.
One challenge is making sure that the different types of data are handled consistently when they are passed between services.
Next week I will focus on combining the assets and sending the video instructions to the rendering service.
title: Text-to-Speech and Media Resources

content:
This week I focused on bringing the different parts of the video-generation workflow together.
The QuizVideoRenderer coordinates the media required for the finished quiz video. This includes the background image, question audio, countdown audio, answer audio and background music.
The VideoInstruction object is used to prepare the instructions and visual overlays. The different resources are represented through VideoFile objects and grouped together in a VideoRequest.
The application then sends this request to the FFmpeg service, which is responsible for rendering the final video.
I also reviewed the VideoController and its POST /video/generate-video endpoint. The endpoint exposes the video-generation process and returns the resulting video with the video/mp4 content type.
This was an important stage because the individual services need to work together in the correct order. A problem with one resource or an incorrectly structured request could affect the complete workflow.
Next week I will focus on testing, documentation and evaluating what is finished and what still needs improvement.
title: Combining the Assets and Rendering the Video

content:
This week I focused on reviewing the overall MyOllama project, testing important functionality and documenting the current implementation.
I reviewed the registration and login flows, database operations, authentication and the main API endpoints.
The tests cover important client-related operations such as creating and finding users, checking passwords, preventing duplicate usernames and validating input. I also reviewed the HTTP tests for registration, login and logout.
Another important part of the work was the API documentation. I wanted the available endpoints, request formats and authentication requirements to be easier to understand.
During the review I also identified functionality that still needs development. The video read, update and delete routes are registered, but their controller methods are currently empty. This means that managing previously generated videos is an area for future work.
Overall, MyOllama now has a structured backend, user authentication, quiz generation through Ollama, text-to-speech through Kokoro and a video-rendering workflow using FFmpeg.
My next priorities would be completing video persistence and CRUD functionality, improving configuration of external services and expanding integration testing.
This week gave me a good opportunity to look at the project as a whole and identify both what has been achieved and what should be improved next.
title: Testing, Documentation and Project Evaluation
